title: Buddhas Zen Brain
speaker: Yuzan Nancy Welch
summary: The talk's main teaching is that by understanding how our brains process emotions and thoughts, we can learn to integrate and accept suffering as part of our experience, rather than trying to separate or eliminate it. By calming the "fight or flight" response that triggers suffering, we can access a more thoughtful state and respond more mindfully to life's challenges. This practice allows us to rewire our brain chemistry to favor calmness, clarity, and compassion, ultimately leading to greater happiness and well-being.

Title for this talk, first I have to explain something.
I have gotten over my fear of computers and really wished I had my computer with me last night, but it's in the shop again.
It seems to spend more time there with me these days.
So it's handwritten notes.
Remember those?
So I was trying to think about the title.
You know, meditation, the brain, and why it is really good to sit still and not think for a while.
And I decided that's the best title right there.

And in case you're worried, I'm not going to talk about how if you really hard and really good meditation, you too could levitate or sleep comfortably on a bed of nails or be buried alive and not need to breathe for a few days.
You've all heard those stories of incredible yogis that can do these things.
And then, I'm sure, however they do it, it certainly must involve an extreme makeover of the brain's chemistry.
But this talk is going to be pretty simple.

It's just sort of a brief overview of the work that's been done in cognitive behavioral psychology, neurology, and exploration with meditators or other contemplative practices to look at what neurologically happens when one meditates or not, when one is used to responding in a certain way to certain situations, and it's no longer appropriate or favorable to do that.
How can you kind of remodel your brain not to react in that same way?
And you really can do that.
So this is sort of a neurological look at what makes for happiness and what makes suffering, which is unavoidable, of course, worse.
We all, suffering is unavoidable, but we interpret it.
This is my version of PowerPoint.
You see these three areas, psychology, neurology, and meditation, or in contemplative practice really.
There's an overlay.
They meet at the center.

And psychology is really our beliefs, self-concept, formed through experience, predisposition, and the developing of mistaken beliefs that become a heuristic in our minds, or a quick and easy way to sum up who we are in relation to the world.
The neurology is the way our brain actually responds to what we're feeling, what we're thinking, how we are interpreting events.

In other words, there's a process of how we feel triggers certain neurological processes or what we think, and then that can, in turn, sort of feed that response or those beliefs, or it can challenge them, help us challenge them.

And that's where it meets in the middle there, meditation, because by the practice of retraining our brain to be less reactive, more present in the present moment, less fearful, and more open to what is, rather than what we've come to expect and may even see, whether it's there or not, because of the way we've trained our brain over time.
The good news is it can change.
You create certain patterns in your brain to begin with and certain ways of responding, and it can change, because that's how they got there in the first place.
Some of the books that I was using to create this talk: the first one is just fantastic, Buddha's Brain.
It's the Practical Neuroscience of Happiness, Love, and Wisdom.
And then this one is Healing Emotions, interviews from the Dalai Lama.
And there's another one that I don't have with me, I loaned it out, another interview type book with the Dalai Lama called Destructive Emotions.
The Dalai Lama has always been interested in science, and so he has really looked into this, and it makes me happy when science and what I'm doing or what I believe or have faith in coincide.
It's like, yeah, not like I have anything to prove, but oh, and this is the Cliff Notes, called The Secrets of Your Brain.
It's a nice little booklet that was put out by US News and World Report.

So in this book, Healing Emotions, there is an interview or dialogue with Jon Kabat-Zinn, who some of you may be very familiar with, since Tim is studying mindfulness-based stress reduction, which is Jon Kabat-Zinn's program of, again, retraining the mind, how we respond to past trauma.

He's specifically currently directing this work towards vets coming home from the Middle East, but mindfulness-based stress reduction is about learning how to bring your body down, calm your body down, not go the same route of fear or confusion.
It can be applied to any situation, not just coming home from a war.
In the one interview, Jon Kabat-Zinn differentiates between curing and healing.
A cure, when and if there is one, can sort of act like magic.
If you're sick, suffering in pain, presto, the physical or psychological symptoms are relieved through a pill, injection, or surgery, or some outside force other than yourself.
Healing means experiencing the suffering on a whole other level.
Through the help of mindfulness meditation, one begins to perceive the body and suffering as a whole unit.
The pain is not an outside invader of the body, but a part of the wholeness of our experience, our body, our mind, and emotions.
Instead of separating these issues into three or more fragments, such as, there's me over here, and I have this pain, and then I have how I feel about the pain, which is I hate it.
It shouldn't be here.
I want to get rid of it.

I want to kill that part of myself, because I don't see it as my part of myself, until I think about it, learn to think about it in a different way, and realize that, wait a minute, this is just another aspect of myself.
What mindfulness does is it integrates, accepts, and sees suffering just as part of the whole living being.
In the Fukan Zenzi Sutra, if I get that right, where Dogen clearly gives us instructions of how to meditate, he says, and I paraphrase, to clear the mind, what one does is to think of not thinking.
How does one think of not thinking?
Non-thinking.
And for the longest time I thought, is that like a koan I'm supposed to chew on the rest of my life?
Think not thinking.
But actually I realize what I believe it means is that to think of not thinking is to not think in our traditional ways.

Non-thinking could also be seen as non-judging, non-analysis, non-attachment to any particular thought or idea, belief or emotion, but rather in meditation we allow any thoughts, feelings that come up just to be, not to cling, hold fast to an idea, a fear or a desire.
Instead we just let it go.
Sitting in meditation is a little bit like practicing for the big game, which is our daily life, moment by moment.
Sitting meditation practice is to practice the not thinking of Dogen's instructions, but to let ideas, emotions, beliefs just rise up and drift away.
It's often used, the mind is the vast sky and our thoughts and emotions are simply the clouds that eventually move.
So it's so freeing to realize that these things, these ideas, emotions, confusions, consternations, they will change if we let them, if we don't cling.
And unfortunately that's true for what we do want to have stay with us, the desirous things that we don't want to go away, but those are going to change too.
With an attitude of non-judgment, non-analysis, non-clinging, you can let those things change, just let everything eventually change.
It'll come back around again.
There's always going to be suffering, and there's always going to be a change in that suffering, and again how we react to it can determine how bad that suffering, light, how we interpret it.
Emptiness is a big concept in Zen, and that's another one I had to chew on.
How can we be empty when we're so full of everything, of life, of perceptions, ideas?

But I heard it explained in a talk here not too long ago that it's not a void, emptiness is not like an abyss, a limitless abyss, but rather it's a letting go, it's a not clinging or adhering to the idea or emotion of the moment, so that you are then empty and thus able to receive what's coming in the next moment, the next feeling, the next perception, new understanding.
And as it is the nature of all life, these things too will change, and once again we can empty ourselves or divest ourselves of our rigid view of life, our way of, the right way of thinking.

We can just let that go, empty ourselves of that, and then have the space to be open to myriad views, ideas, emotions, and this allows us to reach that place of compassion, of truly being able to stand in someone else's shoes and be open to the possibility of others' experience, which is compassion.

My mom used to playfully say when she couldn't make a decision, she would say, "I stand in the draft of an open mind," as if that was a bad thing, and like it was a chilly place she didn't want to stay.
Excuse me.
Okay, so what you may be wondering: what does this have to do with the brain, with neuroscience?
A physician, a neurologist, Daniel Siegel, in his book The Mindful Brain, says that the mind uses the brain to make the mind.
In other words, the mind is what the brain does, and to avoid that trap of dualism you can also flip it around and say the brain is what the mind does, or thinks, feels, or believes.
Our long-ago ancestors, not necessarily our Zen ancestors, but even farther back to the cave people, they really needed to be able to quickly assess danger or threat.
It was pretty scary times back there, and be immediately ready to fight or flee depending on the odds of the situation.
In doing this constant vigilance, constant readiness to fight or flee, over time this response sort of gets engraved, certain responses get engraved in the brain.
They needed to be able to do that in order to take action immediately and have the chemicals in place, quickly access those chemicals to allow them to fight or flee.
What happens, and still happens today, though we usually do not have to fight or flee from a wildebeest, is that even our perception of a threat kicks in what's called the sympathetic nervous system.

I always thought that was kind of funny because sympathetic seems so like, oh nice, but actually what it is, you can think of it as, yeah, it's getting you ready to take action, to take care of yourself, to save yourself.

The sympathetic nervous system is comprised for the most part of certain, these parts of the brain, they call it the hypothalamus, pituitary, adrenal axis, those are the different glands that kick in, as well as the endocrine or hormonal glands.
They all connect, and when they get triggered by a threat, or a perceived threat, or even the absolutely no basis in reality, but scary nonetheless threat, these kick into action.
Now that response was absolutely necessary for humankind to survive at one point.

The sympathetic nervous system would shut down all non-essential bodily functions such as digestion, sexual arousal, as well as compassion, empathy, forethought, basically shutting down the prefrontal cortex where our more complicated thinking takes place.

When it kicks in, it ignites the secretion of adrenaline or epinephrine to increase the heart rate, to move more blood to the muscles, dilates the pupils to gather in more light to see the situation as best you can.

Norepinephrine kicks in and allows blood to move to the larger muscle groups so you can run or wield that club better, and also the bronchials of the lungs dilate in order to process oxygen faster, and cortisol shoots out to actually suppress the immune system in order to reduce inflammation of any wounds that may incur.

That doesn't seem to make sense, but cortisol also suppresses the hippocampus part of the brain, which typically acts as an inhibitor on the amygdala or that whole hypothalamus-pituitary-adrenal axis.

And if these more primitive parts of the brain engage, they take energy away from the more sophisticated, yeah, more sophisticated prefrontal cortex, the part of the brain that has developed much more profoundly in humans than any other animal, and allows us to consider options, have thought, forethought, to think ahead, to imagine, okay, if I do this, what will happen, to make decisions calmly, rationally.
When you're in that fight or flight mode, you don't have time to do that, so the amygdala kicks in, shuts down the prefrontal cortex for the most part, and gets you going in a fear or fight response.

I mentioned, well, I have a friend, unfortunately has, I don't know the long name for this disease, but her prefrontal cortex is actually deteriorating, it's disintegrating, and she can no longer make a decision.
When presented with a decision as simple as do you want orange juice or apple juice, she'll burst into tears.
She cannot process that, she can't make a decision, it's impossible without the nerves and the prefrontal cortex.
It's just amazing.

It's sad, very sad that that's happening to her, but you don't think about how powerful that part of the brain is to allow us to think things through, to make decisions, make choices, even to make the choice to meditate and to quiet the mind, to not think, not keep deciding, not judge, to let things go.
If we didn't have that part of the brain, we couldn't really understand meditation.

Buddha's first noble truth, as we know, is that life is suffering, but it is not necessarily the suffering of intractable pain or profound loss or death, but rather it's the way we assess these conditions that are unavoidable.
Old age, illness, loss, and death are unavoidable.
How we approach them, how we interpret them, will determine how we respond, how we believe, how we react to those things that are going to happen, but we have a choice as to how we react.

We can react sort of blindly, mindlessly, as opposed to mindfully, and increase the suffering by getting that fight or flight mechanism going, trying to not accept what is inevitable: old age, sickness, death.

If we react to a perceived or an inevitable threat of pain as if it were the wildebeest of the caveman days, as if it were something after us, we will neurologically respond as if we were indeed being threatened by outside forces.

Thus your sympathetic nervous system kicks in and leads us around by the nose, which is not fun, because this leads to experiences of anxiety, depression, feelings of helplessness, hopelessness, avoidance, and deep, deep suffering.
Now, there's incredible changes that go on in the body.
This part is called the darts we throw at ourselves.
Some physical discomfort is unavoidable.
It's a crucial signal to take action to protect life and limb, like the pain that makes you pull your hand back from a hot stove.
So mental discomfort is inevitable, too.
For example, as we evolved, growing emotional investments in children and other members of the band or the group motivated our ancestors to keep those carriers of their genes alive.
Understandably, then, we feel distress when our dear ones are threatened and sorrow when they are harmed.
We also evolved to care greatly about our place in the band or in the community of our fellows and in the hearts of others.
So it's normal to feel hurt if you are rejected or scorned by the group.
To borrow an expression from the Buddha, inescapable physical or mental discomfort is the first dart of existence.
As long as you live and love, some of these darts are going to come your way.
The first darts are unpleasant, but then we add our reaction to them.
These reactions are considered the second darts that we throw at ourselves.
Most of our suffering actually comes from the second dart.
Suppose you're walking in a dark room at night and stub your toe on a chair.
Right after that first dart of pain comes a second dart of anger: "Who moved that darn chair?"
Or maybe a loved one has suddenly pulled away from you when you're hoping for some caring.
So in addition to the natural drop in the pit of your stomach, the first dart, you wonder, "What's wrong?
Is you mad at me?"
You can complicate the situation by deciding that you are unwanted and undesirable.
That's the second dart, as a result of having been ignored at that moment, or even long-term: "I'm always treated this way."
That's what I was getting back to, that idea of heuristic thinking.
It's where you just lump everything into one belief: "I will always be rejected."
Then we keep throwing these darts.
Second darts often trigger more darts through associative neural networks.
You might feel guilt about your anger that someone moved the chair, or sadness that you feel hurt yet again by someone you love.
In relationships, second darts can create vicious cycles.
Your second dart triggers reactions from the other person, which sets off more reactions in you, and so on.
If we don't take these conditions mindfully, really pay attention to what we're doing and how we're responding, and interrupt that cycle, it will continue.
It will just dig.
I imagine that in our brains we're digging these pathways, these neural grooves, deeper and deeper without even thinking.
Do I really have to believe these things?
Do I have to keep feeling upset and more upset, getting upset at myself or being upset with my loved ones?
Go on and on.
That can change.
I'm sorry, this is a little unorganized.
It comes from not having my computer, I'm sure.
I have to read my own writing.

If we can calm our raging sympathetic nervous system that gets kicked in by the first dart of "ouch, I hurt," and then how I interpret it, if we can calm that down and access the parasympathetic nervous system, we can actually experience these conditions of suffering with much more calm, more thoughtfulness, again being more open to the possibilities of change.
The parasympathetic nervous system is often called the rest and digest system, as opposed to the fight or flight system of the sympathetic nervous system.

The parasympathetic system corresponds to those lovely neurochemicals such as serotonin, oxytocin in males, vasopressin, which allow for feelings of calmness, closeness, bonding, also protecting our loved ones.

There is more activation of the prefrontal cortex, which is the seat of thoughtfulness, appropriate discrimination, empathy with others, and again compassion, definitely a higher power if one must judge parts of the brain.

In a sort of contradictory way, the ability to discriminate real threats versus perceived threats or results from earlier trauma experience allows us to breathe through it, to wait, to assess, or rather be mindful of what is truly happening now, without the interference of past painful memories or future fear of painful suffering, envisioning of catastrophes, all that stuff that the great human mind can trip itself up with.
So why meditate?

In meditation, what we're doing is practicing letting the thoughts, and the beliefs which accompany them, just be, just pass on through without engaging in them, without believing or judging "is this true or not."
We just let it be.
Meditation is practice in clearing our heads, our minds, of those well practiced but by now automatic responses to outside events.

Allowing yourself to have that space a little bit every day can then allow you to go into your day-to-day life with a more practiced response of calmness, really looking at what's going on now, not getting confused with what happened in the past or what I'm afraid is going to happen in the future.
As we sit in meditation and watch and not judge and just let all these feelings and thoughts go by, we have better practice at doing that in real life, in day-to-day situations.

So rather than reacting to whatever pops up, we're able to see whatever it is for whatever it is, without the automatic assessment of "yikes, run for your life" or, conversely, "yes, this is the way I always want to feel."
Neither is true.
Most times very little threatens us today, but there is the stress of everyday life, disappointments, illness, pain, loss, and nothing wonderful can stick around forever.
Good things change just like the bad things change.
By realizing this, we can judge things as good or bad, desirous or not, as we realize that the judgment helps us cling more closely to those feelings.
In meditation you can just watch yourself react.

You can really take a look at, "Okay, there's that wish, there's that desire, there's that 'oh, I want to go there,' that's a great fantasy," or "oh, that was a great book, I want to reread it" in my head.
And so you're not aware of the moment and you're not really being present.
Allow yourself to be clear-headed, present in this moment.

It is only when we do not practice the acceptance of reality by breathing through all of our thoughts, our fears, our elations, it is only when we do not practice that in meditation that we can remain fearful and threatened by the thoughts that pain will never end, that good things in our life will eventually leave, that everything is just terribly rotten, because we're constantly out of practice of accepting reality just for what it is and realizing that we don't have to get so upset about it, so painfully confused by it all.

If we get caught up in that, our sympathetic nervous system remains on constant engagement, constant alert, which as we know will continue to reinforce itself as we allow our brain to be continually flooded by the fear factors of the neurochemicals epinephrine, norepinephrine, cortisol, and the prefrontal cortex shuts down.

Conversely, if we allow ourselves the everyday practice of meditation, wherein we let thoughts, feelings, etc. arise and move on without reacting, without judging, without clinging, then only then comes the understanding of, "Oh yes, there it is again, I see that fear, I see that worry, I feel that aversion, I feel that desire."
Then we can actually look at reprogramming how we're going to respond to those thoughts, ideas, feelings.

We can reprogram our brain to run more on the parasympathetic nervous system, and yes, it's been proven in studying people in functional MRIs, where they can actually look at what parts of the brain light up when people are doing or told to think certain things or do certain activities.

It's been shown that the more we engage our parasympathetic nervous system, the more the parasympathetic nervous system can become our default neurological system instead of the sympathetic nervous system, which is typically our default response.

Rather than having us on continual vigilance and alarm, fearing what may come rather than what is actually happening right now, in meditation we have the opportunity to practice engaging that parasympathetic nervous system.

Researchers in the field of stress reduction and cognitive behavioral change, such as Marshall Linehan, who operationalized the concepts of mindfulness in an incredible therapy called dialectical behavior training, and John Kabat-Zinn, who uses cognitive restructuring through mindfulness practice, and Daniel Goldman, who in conversation with the Dalai Lama explores the psychology, science and the biological basis of suffering and contentment.

All these researchers and their studies have demonstrated that mindfulness meditation works to reprogram our neurology to move from the habitual reactions based on past trauma, disappointments, pain, fear of what might happen in the future.

We can restructure our brain to have a more open mind, that emptiness of preconceived, to empty out the preconceived beliefs and be open to being refilled with a mindful mind with all the needed neurochemicals that are available to sustain it.
I tried to keep it a little bit simple, although it doesn't sound that way as I was listening to myself.
Neurology to me is just a fascinating thing.
If I wasn't such a lazy student, I probably would have gone into that area.

I just think it's amazing what our brain chemistry can do, and meditation is an integral part of taking control of that, taking control of our own neurology in a sense, and practicing not responding in a habitual, mindless kind of way just because we've always done it.
We've always believed this, so we always will.
Well, that's not true.
We know that.
We know through meditation that we can have a very different response to our experiences, our fears, our emotions, and consequently we can change our neurochemistry.

I think to ignore the sympathetic nervous system would put us in danger in a sense, because we do need to be alert and ready to go into action sometimes in threatening situations.

It's just that when we think we're being threatened and we're really not, that system, like I said, sort of becomes the default system, and then it is out of balance because you're not really giving enough space for the parasympathetic nervous system to kick in.
Yeah, exactly right.
Yeah, but no, we obviously need to be able to have our non-essential functions shut down so we can get out of whatever truly threatening situation it is, or be able to even problem solve.
It's not necessarily running or fighting or constant fleeing.
It can just be a matter of problem solving very difficult, very complicated, knotty, painful problems, and so we need those other chemicals.
We need all of those.
It is, isn't it?
I don't know, but what I've noticed lately is there's a lot of stressed out therapists in this town.
I'm a therapist, and I'll go to one of my friends, "How you doing?"
"I'm so stressed."
I'm like, do you tell your clients this?
I mean, it's great to have compassion for other people being in stress, but to constantly be stressed yourself, I do wonder about that.

Is it our culture that pushes us too far, that constantly reminds us we haven't made enough money, we haven't been beautiful enough, we haven't been successful enough, and so that puts us into that sort of constant threat of "I'm not good enough"? [unclear: "so you're excited"] why is that impulse?
I blame Madison Avenue myself, actually.
I'm serious.
Advertising is an incredibly powerful thing.
It makes us think we need or want or should have certain things, certain experiences, certain relationships, certain looks, certain bank accounts.

And it's not all down to that, but we certainly live in a society that pushes that kind of stuff, so we buy their stuff that they're creating, these advertisers who advertise stuff that we are supposed to want and be happy with.
I know I've probably told this a thousand times, but I had a client in session, an eleven or twelve year old kid who was being used as a ping-pong ball between his parents, unfortunately.
They would try to get him to side with them by giving him stuff.
They had lots of money, and so whatever he wanted, if one parent said no, the other one would go out and buy it for him, and the kid was alone.
I was sort of trying to do family therapy, but it wasn't going real well.
But the kid said something just beautiful.
He said, "Last week, how I really wanted those cards, those magic cards," some sort of wizard game cards or whatever.
I said, "Yeah, I remember, you were really after your mom to get you those."
He said, "Yeah, and she did, and as soon as I got them, I wanted something else."
I was like, you are so lucky to discover that at age twelve.
He realized that this stuff isn't making him happy, because it's not what he needed.
He needed love, he needed peace between his parents, he needed not to be used and bribed.
But anyway, it was just a beautiful, insightful statement by a twelve year old.
It's like, wow, I think there's something to this.
I think I need to look at how much I want things, and do I really want them?
Yeah, like, "You'll feel better, you'll be better, you'll be looked upon in a better light if you buy my stuff."
It's basically what they're saying.
Why is that going to make a difference, when you really think about it?
You had a question?
Yeah.

**Participant:** Well, I was just thinking that too, that it almost seems like the Buddhist philosophy puts forward the idea that if you don't add fuel to the fire, if you don't throw that second dart, then everything's fine, and often it isn't.
**Yuzan Nancy Welch:** Right.
And I'm sorry if I seem to indicate that that's where you're going to find total bliss and happiness.

There are some things where, like I said, we're going to need that sympathetic nervous system to kick in and give us the energy to kind of clear the decks and just see what I need to do to put that fire out if I can, or how can I manage that fire, how can I protect others from that fire.
I do think that just not judging it ourselves isn't going to make it all go away.
Yeah, because there's still going to be problems, there's still war, there's still pain, there's still loss.
Some things can be changed, other things can't.
Just accepting loss is still there.
It's not, to me, I guess it's a question of not adding layer upon layer of more suffering.
It's like my example.
Norman talked to me about my arthritis.
He said, "You basically have a set of symptoms, a set of responses in your body that, for convenience, we've given a name: juvenile rheumatoid arthritis."
But then you can stack all this other stuff on it, like "Oh, I'm deformed, I'm weird, I'm different, I'm ugly, I shouldn't have this, it's not fair, God, you're so mean to me."
All that extra suffering that I realized, through meditation, I was doing to myself.
I was really making it worse.
It still hurts and it will continue to hurt, and sometimes takes me out of play for a while, but I don't have to feel that grinding self-hate I had before about it.
To me, that's the beauty of meditation, of being able to really think, do I really need to look at it that way?
Is there a different way to look at it?
The arthritis is never going to go away until Lee Nelson comes up with a cure.
I keep telling her, "Come on, Lee, hurry, hurry."
She's one of our sangha members, a researcher in Seattle.
Okay, okay, I think I set it up.
